ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Joe Louis

code.originalText: Establishing primary care for persecutory thoughts and poor sleep two weeks after a collapse in the street: a nonjudgmental assessment of cocaine use, the differential of psychosis, a cognitive screen, safety, cardiovascular risk, harm reduction and money worries

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care for persecutory thoughts and poor sleep two weeks after a collapse in the street: a nonjudgmental assessment of cocaine use, the differential of psychosis, a cognitive screen, safety, cardiovascular risk, harm reduction and money worries [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He feels he is being followed and cannot sleep, and wants to feel like himself again. [S]
He is worried about his heart and his mind after collapsing in the street. [S]
He worries about money and does not want his family burdened. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Joe Louis was born Joseph Louis Barrow on May 13, 1914, near LaFayette in Chambers County, Alabama, to Munroe and Lillie Barrow, Alabama sharecroppers; he was one of eleven children. [D]
His family moved to Detroit in the summer of 1926, when he was about twelve, and he took up boxing at a local gym there. [D]

He won the world heavyweight championship on June 22, 1937, by knocking out James J. Braddock, defended it about two dozen times (24 or 25 defenses in different sources), and retired as champion in 1949. [D]

He enlisted in the U.S. Army in January 1942 and served through the Second World War, staging 96 exhibition bouts for the troops and donating the purses of two 1942 fights, nearly $100,000, to the Army and Navy relief societies. [D]

Despite large career earnings, he faced a federal tax debt that by 1956 exceeded $1 million in back income tax, penalties and interest; the debt shaped his finances for many years, and the sources describe its resolution differently. [D]

In 1969 he collapsed on a Manhattan street, shortly after a television interview in New York in late June, and was hospitalized for what was described as a physical breakdown; he later said that the collapse resulted from cocaine use. [D]
In the same period he was troubled by fears of a plot against his life, which a reference biography calls paranoid delusions. [D]
He won 68 of his 71 professional bouts, 54 by knockout. [D]

text.paragraph: 5 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: Retired professional heavyweight boxer and former world champion; Army veteran of the Second World War; now earns an irregular income from paid public appearances [S]
Married; lives with his wife in a rented apartment; asked at first that family not be contacted; no one else is named or given a role in this record [S]

Cocaine: intranasal, most days for about a year, more when traveling for appearances, bought from different sellers; never injected; last use three days before intake. No opioids, no other drugs. Alcohol: a few drinks a week (AUDIT-C 3). Never smoked tobacco [S]
Finances: a federal tax debt from his years as a champion followed him for many years and is now settled, but he has no savings, his income is irregular, and money worries keep him awake [S]
No firearms in the home; drives himself [S]

Strengths and supports: the discipline of a long athletic career, generosity toward others, pride in his Army service and in what his career meant to many people, a quiet dignity and humor, friends from boxing and the Army, and his own decision to come in after the collapse [S]

tr.td: Naloxone 4 mg nasal spray, one spray into one nostril for a suspected opioid overdose, repeated every two to three minutes in the other nostril if needed; two-pack dispensed, with fentanyl test strips and instruction for him and anyone he lives with
One spray as needed for suspected overdose; repeat in 2 to 3 minutes if needed

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert and oriented; courteous and watchful, sitting where he can see the door; speech normal in rate; mood worried and tired; a fixed belief that people are following him and plan to harm him, with partial insight (he wonders aloud whether the cocaine is part of it); no hallucinations; no thoughts of harming himself or anyone else; no confusion; MoCA 25 with points lost on attention and delayed recall after three hours of sleep. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

code.displayName: Physical findings of General status Narrative

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in all activities; has cancelled several appearances in the past month because of fear and fatigue. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-07-13; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert and oriented; courteous and watchful, sitting where he can see the door; speech normal in rate; mood worried and tired; a fixed belief that people are following him and plan to harm him, with partial insight (he wonders aloud whether the cocaine is part of it); no hallucinations; no thoughts of harming himself or anyone else; no confusion; MoCA 25 with points lost on attention and delayed recall after three hours of sleep. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with weekly visits and a phone check in three days. He has persecutory beliefs but no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone, no command hallucinations, no plan to act against the people he fears, and he is caring for himself, so he does not need hospital care now; criteria for urgent care were written down with him (thoughts of harming himself or anyone else, acting on the fears, hallucinations, confusion, chest pain or not sleeping at all for two nights). Risk factors reviewed: cocaine use, persecutory beliefs, poor sleep, money worries and a recent collapse. No firearms in the home. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

A nonjudgmental assessment: DSM-5-TR criteria, the DAST-10 and AUDIT-C, and a urine drug test (with fentanyl) done only with his consent and explained as part of care; person-first language; his own goals first. Guideline: The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2023); Treatment for Stimulant Use Disorders (Treatment Improvement Protocol 33, updated 2021) (2021); Unhealthy Drug Use: Screening (2020) [S]

Addiction psychiatry consultation to settle the diagnosis, advise on an antipsychotic and plan treatment for cocaine use disorder. Guideline: The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2023); The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia (2020) [S]

Differential diagnosis of the psychotic symptoms: follow their course after the last cocaine use; MoCA now and again when he is well; TSH, vitamin B12, HIV and syphilis tests; brain MRI because the symptoms are new after age 50 in a man with years of head impacts; traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis with no clinical test, and no such label is given; a structured assessment that guards against the documented bias toward diagnosing schizophrenia in Black men. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia (2020); National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome (2021); Racial disparities in psychotic disorder diagnosis: A review of empirical literature (2014) [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline saved in his phone, written criteria for urgent care, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Harm reduction: fentanyl can be in cocaine; naloxone nasal spray and fentanyl test strips, never using alone, and the clinic's open door after any use. Guideline: The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2023); Opioid Overdose Reversal Medications (2026) [S]

Cardiovascular risk from cocaine: ECG and creatine kinase today; blood pressure at every visit and a home monitor with twice-daily readings for a week before the four-week visit; call 911 for chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness or tearing pain in the chest or back; beta-blockers avoided while he may still use cocaine. Guideline: The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2023); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025) [S]

Money worries: the clinic social worker helps with a budget, benefits he may qualify for as a veteran, and a free review of his tax records by a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic, with the Taxpayer Advocate Service if any federal tax problem is found. Guideline: Low Income Taxpayer Clinics (2026); Taxpayer Advocate Service (2026) [S]

Family involvement only with his consent: he chooses whom, if anyone, to involve and what may be shared; the clinic contacts no one without his permission unless his life is in danger. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia (2020) [S]

Sleep: regular hours, no cocaine and little alcohol, light in the morning and a dark room at night; no sleeping pill while he may use cocaine or alcohol. Guideline: The ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder (2023) [S]
Referral to addiction psychiatry, Naomi Featherstone-Ibe, MD, ordered 2026-07-13 [S]
